subject: Hi, could you please give me some hints to make such plot? Thank you

messages.author: 4de612b93080ba2f
messages.subject: Hi, could you please give me some hints to make such plot? Thank you
parts:
Hi, 

I am a new to ggplot2. 

I am thinking how to make a plot like this. More specific, I am wondering: 
(1) how to combine the bar plot and the smooth line plot together (and they are in different size)
(2) Previously, I would put the label (A) inside of frame by giving the x and y to certain label, but how to put it out of frame? 

Thank you very much

Tianyi

messages.author: 373beb702917b8b5
messages.subject: Re: Hi, could you please give me some hints to make such plot? Thank you
parts:
Hi Tianyi,

I think this will be moderately complicated, but here is an example to get you started.


## compute values for histogram
wt.dist <- data.frame(hist(mtcars$wt, plot=FALSE)[c("mids", "counts")],
                      group = factor(2, levels = c(1, 2)))

## make a grouping variable so we can get s
mtcars$group <- factor(1, levels = c(1, 2))

## make vales for the smoothers
mtcars$step <- predict(lm(mpg ~ wt, data=mtcars))
mtcars$smooth <- predict(lm(mpg ~ poly(wt), data=mtcars))

## reshape the data putting smoothers in one column
library(reshape2)
mtc <- melt(mtcars, measure.vars = c("step", "smooth"))

## construct the plot
ggplot(mtc, aes(x=wt, y=mpg)) +
    geom_line(aes(y = value, color = variable), data = subset(mtc, variable == "smooth")) +
    geom_step(aes(y = value, color = variable), data = subset(mtc, variable == "step")) +
    geom_histogram(data = wt.dist, aes(x = mids, y = counts), stat="identity") +
    facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y")

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Hi, could you please give me some hints to make such plot? Thank you
parts:
Hi:

Here's a toy example that's in the ballpark of what you were looking for. I wholeheartedly agree with Ista that the task will be a lot simpler if you use a rug plot in place of a histogram.

library(ggplot2)
library(grid)
library(gtable)
# library(gridExtra)
library(plyr)

f <- function(x) x + sin(2 * x) - 0.2 * x^2
DF <- data.frame(x = runif(100, 0, 10))
DF$y <- f(DF$x) + rnorm(100, 0, 0.3)
DF <- arrange(DF, x)  # sort data by x


# Fit a smoothing spline            
# Returns a list of x and y components
s <- predict(with(DF, smooth.spline(x, y, nknots = 8)))
sdf <- as.data.frame(s)

# Fit a third degree polynomial model
pm <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 3), data = DF)

## Base graphic showing the true function, the simulated data 
## and the two fits
curve(f, 0, 10)   # true function
with(DF, points(x, y))
lines(s$x, s$y, col = "blue")
lines(DF$x, predict(pm), col = "darkorange")

## ggplot 

p3 <- ggplot(DF, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
   geom_point() + 
   geom_smooth(size = 1, se = FALSE, aes(color = "poly")) + 
   geom_line(data = sdf, size = 1, aes(color = "smoo")) +
   geom_step(size = 1, aes(color = "stepfun")) +
   geom_rug(sides = "b", color = "darkgreen") +
   scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, by = 2)) +
   labs(title = "Here is a title") + 
   annotation_custom(
     grob = textGrob(label = "A", hjust = 0, gp = gpar(cex = 3)),
     xmin = -1.5, xmax = -1.5, ymin = 3.5, ymax = 3.5) +
   theme(legend.position = c(0.2, 0.25),
         legend.background =  element_rect(fill = "transparent"),
         legend.text = element_text(size = rel(1.2)),
         plot.title = element_text(size = rel(1.5)),
         plot.margin= unit(c(3, 1, 1, 1), "lines")) +
   scale_color_manual(name = "", 
         breaks = c("poly", "smoo", "stepfun"), 
         values = c("darkorange", "blue", "firebrick"),
         labels = c("Cubic polynomial", "Smoothing spline", "Step function"))

g3 <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p3))
g3$layout$clip[g3$layout$name == "panel"] <- "off"
plot(g3)

There are a number of adjustments that needed to be made to make this work:
(1) I needed to generate a factor for the different types of lines inside the ggplot() call and then fine tune the colors and text in scale_color_manual(). It's either this or insert the predictions into the data frame - I chose the latter. This trick is described on p. 109 of the ggplot2 book by Hadley Wickham.
(2) I used annotation_custom() to generate the text label, which also requires an adjustment to turn off masking in the outer plot region so it can be seen. This required a preliminary ggplot_table() call. Ista's suggestion is simpler. This is what I get for not knowing grid very well.
(3) I placed the legend inside the graph; you can see the adjustments that were necessary inside theme(). BTW, rel() inside a theme element function is analogous to cex in base graphics.

This is not a simple graph, nor is the code to create it simple. It uses all kinds of tricks. Fortunately, they're all documented somewhere, either in the ggplot2 book or by Google searches that lead to the archives of either this group or StackOverflow.

I also figured out a way to do it the way you originally intended, but I'd prefer to withhold it until you've shown what you've been able to do in that direction.  Part of the reason for withholding it is because this one is simpler and does enough to indicate the distribution of the x-variable.

Adding the histogram requires several minor modifications to p3 (mostly to remove the x-axis and reduce its reserved space), another ggplot_table() call, a scale_x_continuous() call to coordinate the x-limits in the two graphs, a means of aligning the y-axes and different adjustments to plot.margin in each graph. This is why the geom_rug() suggestion is simpler...and recommended.

Dennis

On Saturday, February 1, 2014 10:39:48 PM UTC-6, Dennis Murphy wrote:
Hi:

Here's a toy example that's in the ballpark of what you were looking for. I wholeheartedly agree with Ista that the task will be a lot simpler if you use a rug plot in place of a histogram.

library(ggplot2)
library(grid)
library(gtable)
# library(gridExtra)
library(plyr)

f <- function(x) x + sin(2 * x) - 0.2 * x^2
DF <- data.frame(x = runif(100, 0, 10))
DF$y <- f(DF$x) + rnorm(100, 0, 0.3)
DF <- arrange(DF, x)  # sort data by x


# Fit a smoothing spline            
# Returns a list of x and y components
s <- predict(with(DF, smooth.spline(x, y, nknots = 8)))
sdf <- as.data.frame(s)

# Fit a third degree polynomial model
pm <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 3), data = DF)

## Base graphic showing the true function, the simulated data 
## and the two fits
curve(f, 0, 10)   # true function
with(DF, points(x, y))
lines(s$x, s$y, col = "blue")
lines(DF$x, predict(pm), col = "darkorange")

## ggplot 

p3 <- ggplot(DF, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
   geom_point() + 
   geom_smooth(size = 1, se = FALSE, aes(color = "poly")) + 
   geom_line(data = sdf, size = 1, aes(color = "smoo")) +
   geom_step(size = 1, aes(color = "stepfun")) +
   geom_rug(sides = "b", color = "darkgreen") +
   scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, by = 2)) +
   labs(title = "Here is a title") + 
   annotation_custom(
     grob = textGrob(label = "A", hjust = 0, gp = gpar(cex = 3)),
     xmin = -1.5, xmax = -1.5, ymin = 3.5, ymax = 3.5) +
   theme(legend.position = c(0.2, 0.25),
         legend.background =  element_rect(fill = "transparent"),
         legend.text = element_text(size = rel(1.2)),
         plot.title = element_text(size = rel(1.5)),
         plot.margin= unit(c(3, 1, 1, 1), "lines")) +
   scale_color_manual(name = "", 
         breaks = c("poly", "smoo", "stepfun"), 
         values = c("darkorange", "blue", "firebrick"),
         labels = c("Cubic polynomial", "Smoothing spline", "Step function"))

g3 <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p3))
g3$layout$clip[g3$layout$name == "panel"] <- "off"
plot(g3)

There are a number of adjustments that needed to be made to make this work:
(1) I needed to generate a factor for the different types of lines inside the ggplot() call and then fine tune the colors and text in scale_color_manual(). It's either this or insert the predictions into the data frame - I chose the latter. This trick is described on p. 109 of the ggplot2 book by Hadley Wickham.
(2) I used annotation_custom() to generate the text label, which also requires an adjustment to turn off masking in the outer plot region so it can be seen. This required a preliminary ggplot_table() call. Ista's suggestion is simpler. This is what I get for not knowing grid very well.
(3) I placed the legend inside the graph; you can see the adjustments that were necessary inside theme(). BTW, rel() inside a theme element function is analogous to cex in base graphics.

This is not a simple graph, nor is the code to create it simple. It uses all kinds of tricks. Fortunately, they're all documented somewhere, either in the ggplot2 book or by Google searches that lead to the archives of either this group or StackOverflow.

I also figured out a way to do it the way you originally intended, but I'd prefer to withhold it until you've shown what you've been able to do in that direction.  Part of the reason for withholding it is because this one is simpler and does enough to indicate the distribution of the x-variable.

Adding the histogram requires several minor modifications to p3 (mostly to remove the x-axis and reduce its reserved space), another ggplot_table() call, a scale_x_continuous() call to coordinate the x-limits in the two graphs, a means of aligning the y-axes and different adjustments to plot.margin in each graph. This is why the geom_rug() suggestion is simpler...and recommended.

Dennis
